newsitem.title: FINLAND: ANGLERS CASTING INTO A FIELD OF DREAMS.
newsitem.headline: ANGLERS CASTING INTO A FIELD OF DREAMS.

text.p: George Blair, 82 years old and water-skiing barefoot with his hands free and the cord between his teeth, is no Olympic athlete.
And neither are the men with fishing rods casting their lines into a field rather than water.
But at the World Games anyone can dream.
In fact, the American's prowess on the water gave some of the water skiing competitors food for thought.
After the world mosquito-killing, wife-carrying and air-guitar playing world championships, Finland is hosting an altogether more serious affair this month. Well, sort of.
"Everybody here has the same story -- we all want to be Olympic sports," said Swiss Roland Hilfiker of the World Air Sports Federation, and a sponsor of parachuting.

Bowling, artistic rollerskating, life-saving, tug-of-war and grenade-throwing are among the would-be Olympic events in the 10-day World Games, which the southern Finnish town of Lahti is hosting this week.
Actually, thankfully for all perhaps, it's not a real grenade they throw in the military pentathlon.
But competitors will be tested on accuracy and distance, and presumably it helps to imagine a bang at the end.
The fifth event of its kind, the Games were last staged in the Netherlands in 1993 to widespread local media derision.
But for the 2,000 participants from 80 countries in 24 different sports, it is no laughing matter.
There is sport and there are pastimes.

"You go tell the bowlers 'we think you guys are playing marbles' and see what happens -- you'll come out like a chopped steak," said South African Ron Froehlich, president of the World Games Federation. Marbles is not a World Games event.
Indeed, bowling gold winner Patricia Schwarz from Germany said she has been competing since she was three years old. "I think practise is very important for a bowler."
To qualify for World Games participation a sport has to have a recognised international federation, and not be included in the Olympic programme. It doesn't have to be easy.
Acrobats flipping each other underarm and overarm -- an event which in the last championship earned the callous moniker "dropping the Chinese boy" -- are, live, a heart-stopping spectacle.

Fortunately this year, the crowd's only gasps at the four-man tempo section in sports acrobatics were in amazement, when young Chinese, Belarussian and Russian men made perfect landings on their partners' crossed palms.
Precision parachute landings may sound a less stunning spectacle, but formation and freestyle skydiving, filmed by a co-jumping cameraman, is pretty knockout.
"We're here to show people that this is not as offbeat as everyone thinks -- it requires as much physical fitness as any sport and more concentration than most," said Hilfiker.
Even casting -- which has everything to do with fishing, albeit without water, and nothing to do with the movies -- makes for far more excitement than regular angling.
Individuals line up with fishing rods in a field, casting and reeling in a tiny weight to hit small round wooden discs accurately and be the first to complete the course.
It does not sound very dynamic, but you have to see it.

"He's a machine, this guy," said American Steve Rajeef, a multi-medalled contestant, as Czech Patrik Lexa cast, reeled, and cast his way to the gold. "In six to eight years in competition no-one's ever seen him miss."

Rajeef, a keen ambassador for the sport who has been casting since he was 10, sees clear similarities in it to Olympic sports like shooting. But he prefers water over a dry course: "Now it's more of a track and field event."
Much closer in many ways to Olympic events, although so far still out of the Olympic picture, is trampolining.

Buzzing around the practice session on Monday was talk of a deal to get it included in gymnastics, making way for limited representation at Sydney in 2000. Competitors say they can already see the difference in each others' motivation.

"There's an Australian here, you can really see she's going to try to be the best," said Briton Sue Challis, a former world champion who said she was coming to the end of her years as a competitor. "You know, she used to be 'just an Aussie'."
"It's a bit like the economy -- you have to see growth as the ultimate aim," said Challis. "Think about the publicity, the finance, the status: you have to get it."

Froehlich, himself a high flyer in the trampoline world, does not want to speculate which World Games events stand the best chance of following baseball, triathlon, taekwondo, softball and women's weightlifting on to the Olympic agenda.
But the pressure is constantly on to make room in the World Games for new variations and events -- like long-distance finswimming. Next up for likely inclusion are seven-a-side rugby and billiards.
"You don't make fun of people's sport," Froehlich said. 120016 GMT aug 97
